newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia parliament slams Chechen deal, drops threat.
newsitem.headline: Russia parliament slams Chechen deal, drops threat.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's parliamentary foes blasted his peace moves in breakaway Chechnya on Friday, saying they would lead to Russia's disintegration, but the deputies retreated from threats to try and impeach the president.

The State Duma, dominated by the communist opposition, also shelved plans to call a vote of no-confidence in the government and failed to approve a final resolution urging a review of Russia's policy in Chechnya. Discussion of the resolution is to continue next week.
Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery at a sanatorium near Moscow, had already made clear he would not be told what to do by the Duma, which under Russia's constitution has limited powers.

The extraordinary Duma session had been convened to debate Yeltsin's decree ordering the pullout of the last two units of army and Interior Ministry troops from Chechnya and the signing of a deal clarifying ties between Moscow and the Caucasus region ahead of elections in January.

"These documents effectively strengthen the judicial disintegration of the country," said Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, predicting that Russia would suffer the same fate as the Soviet Union, dissolved in 1991.
Many deputies, including ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, predicted war in the turbulent region and said the Chechen deal would encourage other regions to secede from the Russian Federation.

Ramazan Abdulatipov, an independent deputy from the Dagestan region bordering Chechnya, said that Chechnya had effectively left the Federation and urged Moscow to focus on improving conditions in regions like his own to avert the spread of separatism there.
Communist deputies said Russia had made all the concessions in its peace talks while the rebels gave nothing in return.
They also complained that Yeltsin's team had failed to consult either the Duma or key ministries and had imposed the new arrangements on them after closed-door talks with the rebels.

However the opposition generally toned its anti-Yeltsin rhetoric during the debate, whose start was delayed by more than an hour while dozens of communists scrambled to find missing cards which activate the electronic voting system.
Just before the session, the Duma's communist speaker Gennady Seleznyov told reporters that neither the issue of impeachment, nor of a no-confidence vote in the government, would be on the agenda.
The move seemed to reflect the fact that Yeltsin, re-elected in July, is in a much stronger position than the Duma.
Under the constitution, any impeachment bid would be a long drawn-out procedure which would have little chance of success.
Any move to bring the cabinet down would give Yeltsin the possibility of dismissing the Duma and calling early elections.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Friday defended the decision to withdraw Russia's remaining troops from Chechnya.
"Their withdrawal is an important step on the road to demilitarisation of the republic and the stabilisation of the regional atmosphere," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, have been killed in the Chechnya conflict since Yeltsin sent troops to try to crush the separatists in December 1994.
Fighting largely ended under a ceasefire last August but no final solution has been found to the central dispute over Chechnya's status -- in or out of Russia.

On Friday Shamil Basayev, leader of a Chechen guerrilla group which seized hostages in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk in June 1995, told reporters in Grozny he would stand for president in the January 27 elections.
